item.title: UMAI: UM Aware Inference with a Frozen Qwen3-ASR
item.description: arXiv:2611.34256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech recognizers often leave filled pauses such as uh and um out of the transcript. Fine-tuning on verbatim transcripts can bring them back, but it can also change the rest of the output. We show that most missing fillers can be recovered from values recorded during a single greedy decoding pass of a frozen recognizer, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B. For each gap between output words, UMAI (UM Aware Inference) pools frame-class posteriors over an audio window located by decoder attention. It combines them with the decoder states through two stages of linear discriminant analysis and calibrates the score by isotonic regression. No parameter is trained by gradient descent. UMAI inserts [uh] and [um] tags and leaves every recognized word unchanged. On the held-out AMI evaluation set, filler F1 rises from 12.2 to 82.6. On the Nyra verbatim benchmark, where the operating threshold was chosen, it rises from 37.2 to 96.5. Total processing time increases by 14%.
item.dc:creator: Gyeongmin Kim

item.title: Psychophysics of Duration Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33176v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Studies of time perception in language models focus mainly on text-based settings. Yet multimodal models are increasingly used for tasks that require perceiving the passage of time, making the limits of their temporal perception important to understand. We measure the limits of duration perception from audio against a human baseline to address this gap. Drawing from psychophysics, we operationalise duration perception as a melody recognition task, testing when a melody becomes unrecognisable as it is slowed down. Of 21 tested models, most cannot recognise well-known melodies without labelled in-context examples. With in-context examples, seven recognise melodies reliably, most peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited: (i) recognition peaks shift with in-context example speed, (ii) melody titles induce prediction bias, and (iii) providing examples with scientific pitch notation does not prevent accuracy declining at long note durations for most models. In humans, the recognition window is a property of the perceiver; in current models, it is largely a property of the prompt.
item.dc:creator: Auss Abbood, Zihao Fu, Nigel Collier

item.title: Evaluating Cine and Tagged MRI-to-Speech Synthesis with Complementary Metrics and MRI-Free Controls
item.description: arXiv:2611.33786v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Relating tongue motion measured with dynamic MRI to the speech it produces could inform rehabilitation after glossectomy. Prior studies have translated cine or tagged MRI into log-mel spectrograms and used the two-dimensional Pearson correlation between predicted and recorded spectrograms (Corr2D) to quantify the acoustic information captured by each imaging modality. However, Corr2D has not been calibrated against MRI-free predictors that preserve basic acoustic structure. Our contribution is an evaluation framework for speech synthesis from cine MRI, tagged MRI and their combination; the synthesis network is held fixed. On identical leave-one-subject-out folds, we compare four trained input configurations with two MRI-free controls: a static mean-spectrum baseline and a time-aligned cohort template. Across 44 subjects (18 after glossectomy) producing two utterances, the cohort template, which never sees an MRI, reached a Corr2D of 0.745 and 0.664. The static baseline, which contains no timing, reached 87 to 89% of that score. No trained configuration outperformed the template on Corr2D, a cepstral distance or ESTOI; seven of the eight fell significantly short on Corr2D. For cine MRI this held across three positional encodings, an encoder temporal-attention module and a training objective matched to the metric. Cine and tagged MRI differed consistently within subjects, although the direction depended on the metric. Absolute Corr2D alone therefore does not show that a model recovers acoustics from the MRI. The two controls are a reusable method: any study can compute them from its own training recordings, so a model's margin over them measures what its images contribute.
item.dc:creator: Karlo Vrancic, Fangxu Xing, Jiachen Zhuo, Maureen Stone, Jerry L. Prince, Jonghye Woo

item.title: InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS
item.description: arXiv:2611.33937v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (Instruct-TTS) renders a target transcript in the manner described by a free-form natural-language instruction, and a good rendition must succeed on three fronts at once: following the instruction, pronouncing the transcript correctly, and sounding natural. Reinforcement learning has become the standard way to post-train such generative models toward human preferences, and TTS systems increasingly adopt it. When the three objectives are optimized together under a single scalar reward, typically with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), training tends to be unstable: the objectives compete, and the shared update drifts toward whichever one is easiest to improve, producing a seesaw among them. We instead adapt on-policy distillation (OPD), which fuses several single-objective teachers by matching their velocity fields on the student's own rollouts. Realizing this for Instruct-TTS first calls for a sound reward on each axis, which we analyze carefully: a distilled Qwen-Omni proxy for the costly Gemini judge, dialect-free data for the WER reward, and DNSMOS in place of the language-biased UTMOS. We then train three single-objective teachers with GRPO and fuse them with OPD, routing each rollout to the instruction-following or WER teacher by its data domain and letting every rollout additionally follow the MOS teacher for quality. This lets instruction following and intelligibility improve together without a trade-off, but the quality target conflicts with instruction following, so following it additively reintroduces the seesaw. We therefore propose conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction that opposes the primary objective before fusing, and show that it markedly reduces the instruction-following/quality trade-off. The fused model improves over scalar-reward GRPO on all three objectives at once.
item.dc:creator: Haitao Li, Tian Tan, Yuguang Yang, Guanrou Yang, Wenhao Guan, Chenglin Li, Shan Yang, Xie Chen

item.title: Beat This! Live - Online Beat and Downbeat Tracking by Predicting the Future
item.description: arXiv:2611.34277v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.
item.dc:creator: B\'ank Juh\'asz, Gerhard Widmer, Jan Schl\"uter

item.title: Music Similarity Estimation from Jukebox Embeddings
item.description: arXiv:2611.34346v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Content-based music similarity estimation aims to provide a measure of similarity between music audio recordings, disregarding any associated metadata. This has potential applications in e.g. cold-start music recommendation scenarios, where there is no user interaction data. In this work, we propose JukeSim, a new approach to estimating musical similarity based on embeddings created by Jukebox, a generative music model. In evaluations on multiple datasets, we find that JukeSim performs on par with an existing learning-based approach, and both outperform the best hand-designed approaches, which had never been compared to recent work before. Even though the required compute for JukeSim is higher than for other measures, we demonstrate the viability of utilizing generative embeddings for this task, encouraging further research.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Grafinger, Gerhard Widmer, Jan Schl\"uter

item.title: Investigation of generalization to unseen audio generation models in audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.34626v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Text-to-audio generation (TTA) requires reliable evaluation of semantic alignment between generated audio and input text. Existing learning-based alignment-score prediction models have been evaluated only on audio generated by models included in the training data, leaving their generalization to unseen generation models unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the generalization of audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction models to unseen TTA models and introduce adversarial training using a generation-model classifier with a gradient reversal layer (GRL). Experimental results show that pretrained audio encoders capture generation-model-specific characteristics and that alignment-score prediction performance degrades on audio generated by unseen TTA models. Applying the GRL improves prediction performance in some settings, although its effectiveness in suppressing generation-model-specific information is limited.
item.dc:creator: Yuki Okamoto, Noriyuki Tonami, Takao Kawamura, Keisuke Imoto, Ryotaro Nagase, Riki Takizawa, Minoru Kishi, Shinnosuke Takamichi

item.title: FSC-Net: Integrating Fast Fourier Convolutions and Progressive Learning for Speech Bandwidth Extension
item.description: arXiv:2606.06962v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speech bandwidth extension (BWE) aims to reconstruct high-fidelity wideband audio from narrowband inputs. While recent approaches have made significant progress, they often struggle to reconstruct realistic high-frequency phase and harmonic structures, leading to perceptual artifacts. In this paper, we propose FSC-Net (Full-Spectrum Context Network), a parameter-efficient architecture designed to explicitly model cross-band harmonic dependencies. By integrating Fast Fourier Convolutions (FFCs) into a complex spectral mapping framework, FSC-Net expands its receptive field to the entire spectrum, capturing long-range frequency interactions effectively. To address the ill-posed nature of high-frequency generation, our novel frequency-progressive learning curriculum guides the network to reconstruct spectral details from coarse to fine. Experimental results on the VCTK and unseen EARS datasets demonstrate that FSC-Net delivers consistently strong reconstruction quality and generalization, particularly in the challenging VCTK 4 kHz-to-48 kHz task. Compared to scaled-up baselines, our model attains leading LSD and PESQ scores while maintaining a highly compact parameter footprint (1.54 M).
item.dc:creator: Xinan Chen, Xiaobin Rong, Qinwen Hu, Kai Chen, Jing Lu

item.title: Speaker-Aware Temporal Aggregation Strategies on Segment Representations for Depression Detection in Dyadic Interaction: A Benchmark Study
item.description: arXiv:2607.02904v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speech-based depression detection compresses features from short audio segments into one speaker-level decision, a step called temporal aggregation rarely studied on its own. Most benchmarks fix a single self-supervised encoder and a single hand-picked layer, so a reported gain may reflect the pipeline rather than the aggregation method itself. We introduce DEPOOL, a controlled benchmark that compares six aggregation architectures with six frozen speech backbones on an English and a Mandarin depression corpus, where each configuration learns which backbone layers matter rather than fixing one by hand. Across the resulting 72-configuration grid, a third of configurations collapse into predicting a single class for every speaker, a failure tied to the backbone as much as to the method, and the architecture that is most stable in a single seed run becomes unreliable when training repeats across seeds. Robustness to backbone and seed, rather than average accuracy across a single pipeline, should be a first-class benchmarking criterion for temporal aggregation in clinical speech.
item.dc:creator: Anisha Pattanayak, Huang-Cheng Chou, Shrikanth Narayanan, Sudarsana Reddy Kadiri

item.title: Layer-wise Cross-Lingual Depression Detection from Speech: Analysis with Contrastive Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2607.02920v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Significant disparities exist in the diagnosis and clinical presentation of depression across different linguistic populations. Speech-based depression detection performs well mono lingually, but cross-lingual generalization remains an open challenge. A key reason is that prior work uses segment-level random splits without speaker grouping, leading to identity leakage that inflates reported metrics. We propose CLeaD, a supervised contrastive alignment framework that maps WavLM embeddings from English and Mandarin into a shared clinical space, without parallel data or target-language fine-tuning. Evaluating 52 Mandarin speakers, contrastive alignment modestly outperforms the baseline (F1: 0.640 vs. 0.622) under leave-one speaker-out evaluation. It also improves depressed-class recall at intermediate layers (7-8), though the small test set limits generalizability. Two findings remain robust: model scaling degrades cross-lingual performance while improving monolingual English, and a controlled within-pipeline ablation shows that speaker identity leakage alone inflates Mandarin F1 from 0.628 to 0.856, an artifact we reproduce and quantify.
item.dc:creator: Anisha Pattanayak, Hanie Kang, Huang-Cheng Chou, Shrikanth Narayanan, Sudarsana Reddy Kadiri

item.title: Emilia2: A Large-Scale Dataset for Controllable Long-Form Speech Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.13614v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generating long-form speech requires models to keep content, speaker identity, turn-taking, and expressive style consistent over time. Yet most open training corpora contain examples lasting only tens of seconds and open long-form benchmarks cover at most two speakers per recording. We introduce Emilia2, a 229K-hour multilingual dataset for controllable long-form speech generation. From in-the-wild data, Emilia2 constructs short utterances, single-speaker long-form speech, and multi-speaker dialogues, preserving transcripts, speaker identities, pauses, and acoustic transitions. Examples longer than five minutes account for 50.0% of single-speaker long-form hours and 66.8% of dialogue hours. To support expressive control, Emilia2 provides natural language instructions for 4.77M examples and nonverbal-vocalization tags for 933K examples. We also introduce Emilia2-testset, 23 hours of bilingual recordings of up to 30 minutes and four speakers, each speaker paired with reference audio. We train autoregressive (AR) and non-autoregressive (NAR) models on Emilia2. Our 0.6B-backbone NAR model achieves the lowest Chinese CER and English WER on TTSD-Eval (5.27%/9.93%) among compared systems, while our AR model is on par with Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-VD on InstructTTSEval (zh/en: 76.2/78.3 vs. 77.1/77.9). These results validate Emilia2 as a comprehensive data foundation for long-form speech generation and minute-scale expressive control. Demo: https://charlesnii.github.io/Emilia2-demo/.
item.dc:creator: Qinke Ni, Dekun Chen, Junwen Qiu, Huan Liao, Xu Li, Xingwen Han, Wan Lin, Kunyu Feng, Yuxiang Wang, Yusheng Mu, Chaoren Wang, Yingda Shen, Mingjie Chen, Haolong Zheng, Xulin Fan, Mark A. Hasegawa-Johnson, Zhizheng Wu
